title_en: A Goldman M&A Banker Helped Bring the Olympics to Los Angeles
title_zh: Goldman Sachs 并购主管 Gene Sykes：如何把奥运会带到 Los Angeles
subtitle_zh: Gene Sykes 谈 LA28 奥运如何私人出资，以及 AI 浪潮下的并购与媒体交易。
description: A Goldman M&A Banker Helped Bring the Olympics to Los Angeles

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios。

turns.en: Podcasts.
turns.zh: 播客。

turns.en: Radio. News. Hello and welcome to another episode of the OddLots Podcast. I'm Tracey Alloway.
turns.zh: 广播。新闻。大家好，欢迎收听新一期的 OddLots 播客。我是 Tracey Alloway。

turns.en: And I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: Joe, we are here in lovely Huntington Beach at the Future Proof Conference.
turns.zh: Joe，我们现在人在风景宜人的 Huntington Beach，参加 Future Proof 大会。

turns.en: I love coming to this conference.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢来这个大会了。

turns.en: You can't complain.
turns.zh: 这你没什么可抱怨的。

turns.en: The beach is right there.
turns.zh: 海滩就在那儿。

turns.en: They do such a good job.
turns.zh: 他们办得非常出色。

turns.en: Every time I'm here, the only thought I have is they have brought heaven on earth. And the only mystery I have is why there are people, you know, you think about like the great migration west. It's like, imagine stopping in Nebraska. You could have gone a little bit further and you could have been in California.
turns.zh: 每次我来这儿，脑子里唯一的念头就是他们把人间天堂搬到了地上。唯一让我想不通的是，为什么不是所有人都住这儿——你想想当年的西部大迁徙（great migration west），就好比说，你居然在 Nebraska 停下了。你其实可以再往前走一点，就到 California 了。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And it's like it was right there. And the question I have is, why doesn't everyone live here?
turns.zh: 就是说，它明明就在那儿。我想问的是，为什么不是所有人都住这儿？

turns.en: OK, well, we made it to California. It's our fourth year at this particular event. And we do, in fact, have the perfect guest. We recorded an episode live on stage with Gene Sykes. He is the co-head of Global M & A at Goldman Sachs, a longtime partner and also the president of the U.S. Olympic Committee. So take a listen.
turns.zh: 好吧，反正我们是到 California 了。这是我们第四年来参加这个活动。而且我们确实请到了最完美的嘉宾。我们在台上现场录制了一期节目，嘉宾是 Gene Sykes。他是 Goldman Sachs 全球并购（Global M&A）的联席主管，是资深的合伙人，同时也是美国奥委会（U.S. Olympic Committee）的主席。那我们来听听吧。

turns.en: Gene, thank you so much for joining us.
turns.zh: Gene，非常感谢你来做客。

turns.en: Happy to be here.
turns.zh: 很高兴来到这里。

turns.en: Let's start really simple.
turns.zh: 我们先从最简单的问起。

turns.en: We can save the tough questions for the end, but let's start really simple.
turns.zh: 难的问题可以留到最后，先从简单的开始。

turns.en: You wear many hats, Goldman, the Olympics. What are you up to now?
turns.zh: 你身兼数职，Goldman、奥运会。你现在都在忙些什么？

turns.en: Tell us who you are, maybe. Okay, I'm still a Goldman Sachs partner after many, many years. I think I've been a partner at Goldman Sachs for half my life. And I work on technology and media, healthcare and other things. And because I've been around for a long time, I get to do more or less what I want, which is to give people advice who need advice and value it and work with all of our teams and spend a lot of time mentoring people. So that's the Goldman part of my time. The other half of my time or more is spending time in everything related to the Olympic and Paralympic ecosystem. So I was the head of the bid when we bid for the games for Los Angeles, originally for 2024. We were awarded the 2028 games, you know, less than two years. We'll have the Olympic and Paralympic games right here in Southern California. But then four years ago, I became the chair of the board of the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee. So I spent a lot more time now thinking about how do we create Team USA so that our athletes are always the highest performing athletes in any of these Olympic or Paralympic events. And then about two and a half years ago, I became a member of the International Olympic Committee. So I sort of see the entire Olympic, Paralympic landscape.
turns.zh: 跟我们说说你是谁吧，也许。好的，做了这么多年，我现在仍然是 Goldman Sachs 的合伙人。我觉得我在 Goldman Sachs 当合伙人的时间已经占了我人生的一半。我做的是科技和媒体、医疗健康等等领域。因为我入行很久了，所以基本上可以做自己想做的事，也就是给那些需要建议、也看重建议的人出主意，和我们所有的团队合作，还花很多时间去做导师、带年轻人。这是我花在 Goldman 上的那一半时间。另一半甚至更多的时间，都花在了跟奥运和残奥生态相关的一切事情上。当初 Los Angeles 申办奥运会——最早是申 2024 年——我就是申办委员会的负责人。后来我们拿到了 2028 年奥运会的主办权，你知道，不到两年之后，奥运会和残奥会就会在这里、在 Southern California 举行。再后来，四年前，我当上了美国奥运与残奥委员会（U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee）的董事会主席。所以我现在花更多时间在琢磨，我们怎么打造出 Team USA，让我们的运动员在任何一届奥运或残奥赛事里都是表现最出色的那批人。然后大概两年半以前，我又成了国际奥委会（International Olympic Committee）的委员。所以整个奥运、残奥的版图，我基本上都看在眼里。

turns.en: When I think about the Olympics, I'm not big into sports. OK, like I'm not not Sidney Sweeney, like sports, sports, sports, sports. Right. I just see the Olympics. They're kind of interesting. What counts to you as a successful Olympic Games? Is it keeping the cost down as much as possible?
turns.zh: 说到奥运会，我这人不太痴迷体育。好吧，我不像 Sidney Sweeney 那样满脑子都是体育体育体育。我就是觉得奥运会还挺有意思的。对你来说，怎样才算一届成功的奥运会？是尽可能把成本压下来吗？

turns.en: The vibes?
turns.zh: 看氛围（vibes）？

turns.en: What does it actually look like?
turns.zh: 它到底长什么样？

turns.en: Successful Olympic Games has to be a games that everyone says, I'll never forget this. This is an incredible experience. And I only saw it here. This is the only way I can see all of these incredible athletes in these kinds of competitions and see them in one place at the same time. And when you say you're not a sports fan, how many people are Alyssa Liu fans with figure skating who wouldn't call themselves sports fans? The other thing about the Olympics most people don't realize is the Olympics are the one sports experience that skews toward women more than toward men.
turns.zh: 一届成功的奥运会，必须是那种每个人都会说'我这辈子都忘不了'的奥运会。这是一段难以置信的体验，而且我只有在这里才看得到。这是我唯一能一次看到这么多顶尖运动员、在同一时间、同一个地方同场竞技的机会。你说你不是体育迷，可你想想，花样滑冰的 Alyssa Liu 有多少粉丝是那种自己都不认为算体育迷的？关于奥运会，还有一点是大多数人不了解的：奥运会是唯一一项观众里女性占比高于男性的体育赛事。

turns.en: Really?
turns.zh: 真的吗？

turns.en: I would not have guessed that at all. You know, we obviously just hit the World Cup in the U.S., but that's like one sport. There are probably like 12 stadiums or something like that. There's one governing body. Can you give us a feel for essentially like the sprawl of the organization and how many different, maybe we call them stakeholders, have to be brought in to make an Olympics go well?
turns.zh: 这一点我完全没想到。你知道，我们刚在美国办完世界杯（World Cup），但那只是一项运动。大概也就十二座体育场之类的。只有一个管理机构。你能不能给我们讲讲，这个组织到底摊子铺得有多大，要让一届奥运会办得顺利，得把多少不同的——我们也许可以叫利益相关方（stakeholders）——都拉进来？

turns.en: Sure. So in contrast to the World Cup, we had 104 matches during the World Cup between Mexico, the U.S. and Canada. 16 different stadiums were hosts for the events.
turns.zh: 当然。跟世界杯对比一下，世界杯期间我们在 Mexico、美国和 Canada 之间一共踢了 104 场比赛，有 16 座不同的体育场承办了赛事。

turns.en: That's enough.
turns.zh: 那也够多了。

turns.en: Not that much. 600 athletes, let's say. I mean, not that many athletes. By comparison, in the Olympic and Paralympic Games, when you put the two together, we'll have 17,000 athletes. We'll have something like 900 separate events, medal events. It's enormous. We'll sell 15 million tickets between the Olympic and the Paralympic Games in Los Angeles. The World Cup sold 6.5 million tickets. So it's a significantly bigger and more complicated experience than the World Cup. You know, it's not everything, but it's maybe 90% of everything you can imagine in the world of sports.
turns.zh: 其实不算多。运动员嘛，就说 600 人吧，我是说，没那么多运动员。相比之下，奥运会和残奥会如果合在一起算，我们会有 17,000 名运动员，大概 900 个单独的项目、夺牌项目。规模极其庞大。Los Angeles 的奥运会加残奥会，我们会卖出 1,500 万张门票。世界杯卖了 650 万张。所以这比世界杯要大得多、也复杂得多。你知道，它不是涵盖一切，但大概相当于你能想象到的体育世界里 90% 的东西。

turns.en: So if there is one thing I know about the Olympics, it's that people like to complain about the cost, right? And empty stadiums and finding uses for all this infrastructure that was built afterwards. What's the funding mix actually supposed to be for the 2028 LA games? Because I keep reading headlines saying the first privately funded games. I'm not sure that's true.
turns.zh: 如果说奥运会有一件事我是知道的，那就是大家都爱吐槽成本，对吧？还有空荡荡的体育场，以及事后给这些建好的基础设施找用途。2028 年 Los Angeles 奥运会的筹资结构到底应该是怎样的？因为我老看到标题说这是第一届私人出资的奥运会。我不确定这说法对不对。

turns.en: Well, it's essentially privately funded in that there's no government support to put the games on, with the exception of the federal government playing a role in security and security-related logistics, things of that sort. You can't do that without the federal government, with everybody in the world being here. There are 206 countries that will send teams to the Olympic Games. So it's quite a security event for sure. The idea of the privately funded games in Southern California, we have the best sports infrastructure here of any city in the world. We have more stadia and arenas and world-class places where sports already takes place. So we don't have to build anything. We're not building a village for the athletes, you know, which is what Paris had to do because we've got such great residences at UCLA. We're going to keep all the athletes at UCLA and UCLA houses many more students in a regular year than we'll need to house athletes during the games. So this is the ideal setting to have a games like this. And that makes it a lot easier to plan and to execute.
turns.zh: 嗯，它基本上算是私人出资的，意思是办这届奥运会没有政府出钱，唯一的例外是联邦政府会在安保以及安保相关的后勤这类事情上出份力。全世界的人都要来这里，没有联邦政府你可办不成。会有 206 个国家派队参加奥运会。所以这肯定是一场安保大事。至于在 Southern California 办一届私人出资的奥运会这个构想——我们这里拥有全世界任何城市里最好的体育基础设施。我们有更多的体育场、场馆和世界级的、本来就在举办体育赛事的场地。所以我们什么都不用建。我们不用给运动员盖奥运村，你知道，这正是 Paris 不得不做的事，因为我们在 UCLA 有非常棒的宿舍。我们会把所有运动员都安排在 UCLA，而 UCLA 在平常年份住的学生，比奥运会期间我们要安排的运动员还多得多。所以这里是办这样一届奥运会的理想之地。这也让规划和执行都容易了很多。

turns.en: I have some friends in L.A. and they have a house here.
turns.zh: 我在 L.A. 有些朋友，他们在这儿有房子。

turns.en: And they're like, by the way, we're thinking of renting out the house to people coming.
turns.zh: 他们就那种，'顺便说一句，我们在考虑把房子租给来的人。'

turns.en: But if you wanted to come, we would let you stay in the house.
turns.zh: '但如果你想来的话，我们就让你住这房子。'

turns.en: They would give up the money for you, Joe. Yeah.
turns.zh: 他们愿意为你放弃那笔租金，Joe。是啊。

turns.en: But to my mind. That's a good deal. I take it.
turns.zh: 但要我说，这可是笔划算的买卖。我接受。

turns.en: I know it's a good deal.
turns.zh: 我知道这是笔划算的买卖。

turns.en: But the flip side is like, oh, my God, the traffic. And the standing in lines, these are some of my least favorite things to do in the world. Make the argument to me that if I come down to L.A. for the Olympics, I will actually find it a smooth experience rather than an experience where I'm spending half the day in lines. And then in the week up to it, logging into eight different sites just to be able to buy a ticket.
turns.zh: 但另一面是，天哪，那交通。还有排队。这些是全世界我最不喜欢的几件事。你跟我说说，如果我来 L.A. 看奥运会，我到底会不会觉得这是一次顺畅的体验，而不是半天都在排队，然后在那之前的一周里还得登录八个不同的网站才买得到一张票。

turns.en: I mean, L.A.
turns.zh: 我是说，L.A. 嘛。

turns.en: Traffic is bad at the best of times, right?
turns.zh: 交通就算在最好的时候也很糟，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Well, I don't know. The best of times, it's not bad.
turns.zh: 嗯，这我可不好说。最好的时候，其实没那么糟。

turns.en: Four in the morning, the best of times, it's not bad.
turns.zh: 凌晨四点，最好的时候，确实没那么糟。

turns.en: To give you some comfort, people said the same thing about the 84 games. We hosted the games in 1984. A lot of people said, I'm going to leave because the traffic is going to be so bad. And the traffic was totally manageable. The thing about LA and traffic is if you tell people in advance something is happening, stay off the roads, and they all know about it. They know where it's going to be and they know when it's going to happen. They do. People behave based on what they know and what they're expecting to happen. That plus the fact that you're going to have a lot of very elaborate planning for how you get traffic moving around through what will be called Olympic lanes. Today, they're high occupancy vehicle lanes, HOV lanes.
turns.zh: 给你们一点安慰吧，当年大家说起 84 年奥运会也是这么讲的。我们在 1984 年办过奥运会。很多人说，'我要走了，因为交通会糟透了。'结果交通完全应付得来。关于 L.A. 的交通，有一点是：如果你提前告诉大家某件事要发生，叫他们别上路，而所有人又都知道这回事——他们知道在哪儿、知道什么时候发生——他们真的会照着做。人们会根据自己知道的、以及自己预期会发生的事来行动。再加上，你们还会有非常周密的规划，来安排车流怎么绕行，走那些将被称作'奥运车道（Olympic lanes）'的道路。今天，它们是载多乘客的车道，也就是 HOV 车道。

turns.en: Oh, yeah. Am I going to have to download three apps to buy a ticket or whatever?
turns.zh: 哦，对。我是不是还得下载三个 App 才能买到票什么的？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: One app, you're either going to buy your tickets in advance. Literally half the tickets have already been sold. So you want to register for the tickets. The next time the tickets are available is next year. Okay. So I think tickets you'll get in advance. You don't have to go to a bunch of different apps. You'll have one app, which will tell you what's happening, where to go. It'll be easy for you to see it. And I don't think you'll have many lines. I think the venues actually will be really great. Remember, all these venues already do sports.
turns.zh: 一个 App。你要么就提前买票。说实在的，一半的票已经卖出去了。所以你想登记买票的话——下一次放票是明年。好，所以我觉得票你会提前买到。你不用去下一堆不同的 App。你就一个 App，它会告诉你正在发生什么、该去哪儿。看起来会很方便。而且我觉得你也不会排太多队。我觉得那些场馆其实会非常棒。别忘了，所有这些场馆本来就在办体育赛事。

turns.en: You're selling me.
turns.zh: 你都快把我说服了。

turns.en: Well, think about it. All of these venues have enormous events all the time that people who operate them know exactly what to do.
turns.zh: 嗯，你想想看。所有这些场馆一直在办大型活动，运营它们的人完全清楚该怎么做。

turns.en: You already have accommodation, Joe.
turns.zh: Joe，你住的地方都已经有啦。

turns.en: You should just do it. Just do it.
turns.zh: 你就该去。就去。

turns.en: So I know it's not a perfect apples for apples comparison, but, you know, the World Cup was the sprawling, complicated sports event. When you look back at the summer, is there anything with your Olympics board membership hat on that you would have done differently when it comes to the World Cup?
turns.zh: 我知道这不算完全对等的比较，但你知道，世界杯是那种摊子铺得很大、很复杂的体育赛事。回过头看这个夏天，戴上你奥运董事会成员那顶帽子，关于世界杯，有没有什么你会做得不一样的地方？

turns.en: Certainly, I would have been careful about calling the president for a red card violation. That probably wasn't the best thing for the World Cup's image. Having said that, the experience for Americans was awesome. I mean, the fact that people in the United States could see soccer, which everybody else calls football, it's not really our sport, but they could feel like they were part of it with the very, very best athletes in the world. I think it actually really transformed Americans' view of that sport. and they'll appreciate that sport differently than they ever have before. Plus, the people who came and they were cheering for their teams, they found America to be incredibly welcoming and Americans to be exciting and interesting. And the image that we Americans made of ourselves to the rest of the world was incredibly positive and constructive, even when the public image of American politicians may be very mixed. So I think it was a huge positive.
turns.zh: 当然，我会当心一点，别为了一个红牌犯规就给总统打电话。那大概不是对世界杯形象最有好处的事。话虽如此，对美国老百姓来说，这段体验棒极了。我是说，美国人能看到足球——别的国家都管它叫 football，虽然它在我们这儿真算不上是我们的运动——但他们能感觉自己身在其中，和全世界最顶尖的运动员在一起。我觉得这真的改变了美国人对这项运动的看法，他们会以一种前所未有的方式去欣赏这项运动。另外，那些来给自家球队加油的人，他们发现美国极其好客，美国人既热情又有意思。而我们美国人给世界其他地方留下的形象，是极其正面、极具建设性的，哪怕公众对美国政客的看法可能褒贬不一。所以我觉得这是一件大大的好事。

turns.en: I don't think in my lifetime there has been a single sporting event that the week before.
turns.zh: 我这辈子还从来没有过哪一届体育赛事，是在开赛的前一周——

turns.en: You see all these headlines. The stadiums aren't ready.
turns.zh: 你会看到满屏这样的标题：体育场还没准备好。

turns.en: The grass isn't growing. The seats are still being installed. And then it all works out fine. And then in more recent sporting events, you're like, well, the international tourists aren't coming. They don't like the vibes in the United States, etc. Based on what you've seen so far, and you mentioned the first batch of ticket sales, do you have any reason to think that The environment in the U.S., which we could talk about in a million different ways, is going to affect attendance in one way or another.
turns.zh: 草还没长出来。座位还在装。结果呢，一切最后都顺顺利利。而到了更近的这些体育赛事，你又会想，'嗯，国际游客不来了。他们不喜欢美国的氛围'等等。基于你到目前为止看到的，还有你提到的第一批门票销售，你有没有什么理由认为——美国的环境，这个我们可以从一百万个不同角度去聊——会以某种方式影响到场人数？

turns.en: No. The ticket sales, first of all, have been incredibly positive. As soon as they were offered, everything was sold. And you said they're high priced. They are high priced. But they are priced at the market. And it's going to take a lot of ticket sales to actually pay for these games. So I don't really apologize for the fact that they're high priced, except to say, if you want to see the very, very best in sports, in any sport, at one place, all at a very compressed period of time, it's it's a premium priced experience.
turns.zh: 没有。首先，门票卖得极其火爆。一放出来，全都卖光了。你说它们价格高。价格是高。但它们是按市场定的价。而要真正为这届奥运会买单，需要卖出很多很多票。所以我其实不太会为票价高这件事道歉，我只想说：如果你想在一个地方、在一段极其紧凑的时间里，看到任何一项运动里最顶尖的较量，那这就是一种高端定价的体验。

turns.en: Wait i didn't say they're high priced i have no concept of what a fair value is for a sports ticket but okay let me try to segue between the olympics and the media landscape but you have to raise money for this right through media sponsorships and air rights and things like that what's the demand like that you're seeing so far.
turns.zh: 等等，我可没说它们价格高，我对一张体育门票的合理价值是多少完全没概念。好吧，让我试着在奥运会和媒体版图之间做个衔接。但你得为这事筹钱，对吧？通过媒体赞助、转播权等等。到目前为止，你看到的需求怎么样？

turns.en: Well, the demand is great. So some of this is done. It's pre-baked. The International Olympic Committee sells media rights for all the games. They do it years in advance. NBC is the media rights holder for the United States. They've got a deal that now goes through 2036. We don't even know where the games are going to be in 2036. And they're committed to be the media partner in the United States for those games. That's a significant amount of money. It's a billion and a half dollars or more per games to have the rights in the United States. Then the IOC also sells a bunch of sponsorships to people like Coca-Cola and Visa and Samsung. You've seen the names of these companies around every one of the Olympic Games. But then the domestic organizers get the opportunity to sell more rights. And so they've sold rights to Starbucks and Uber and Google. And so you get the idea that there is huge corporate interest in sponsoring these games. They want to be part of it because they know this is going to be the biggest event in the history of the world. And I mean, that sounds crazy, but I think it will be that. And if you're here for it, you're going to say, I have just been part of something which is going to be remembered forever.
turns.zh: 嗯，需求非常旺。这里面有一部分是早就定好的、是预先谈妥的。国际奥委会负责出售所有奥运会的媒体版权，而且是提前很多年就去卖。NBC 是美国的媒体版权持有方。他们的合约现在一直签到 2036 年。我们连 2036 年奥运会在哪儿办都还不知道，而他们已经承诺要做那届奥运会在美国的媒体合作伙伴。这可是一大笔钱，每届奥运会在美国的版权就是 15 亿美元甚至更多。此外，国际奥委会还会卖出一批赞助权，买家像 Coca-Cola、Visa、Samsung 这些。每一届奥运会你都能看到这些公司的名字。然后，本地的组委会还有机会卖出更多权益。所以他们已经把权益卖给了 Starbucks、Uber 和 Google。所以你能感觉到，企业界对赞助这些奥运会有巨大的兴趣。他们想参与其中，因为他们知道这将会是世界历史上最大的一场活动。我是说，这话听起来很夸张，但我觉得它真会是这样。而如果你身在其中，你会说，'我刚刚参与了一件会被永远记住的事。'

turns.en: So I lied before when I said I don't like sports. I do like football slash soccer. But one of the criticisms of of FIFA was rampant commercialization in the games, right? So, you know, 15 minute water breaks so that there are more ad sales and stuff like that. Are you thinking of additional ad or sponsorship opportunities for the Olympics?
turns.zh: 我前面说我不喜欢体育，那是撒谎。我确实喜欢 football，也就是足球。但对 FIFA 的批评之一，就是赛事里泛滥的商业化，对吧？比如说搞 15 分钟的补水暂停，好多卖点广告之类的。你有没有在为奥运会考虑更多的广告或赞助机会？

turns.en: Well, definitely not like that. So the Olympics are famous for having clean venues. If you've been in Olympic games and you see the field of play, you'll notice there's no corporate advertising anywhere in the field of play. Anywhere you see the athletes competing, there's no corporate advertising at all. And that's kind of an Olympic rule. And everyone abides by the rule. And if there's going to be any sort of advertising, it's the brand and the brand is offstage. It may be where the athletes are putting a helmet on or something. Yeah. But it's very, very distinctive in that it's totally clean. And you feel like, wow, this is all about the sports and all about the athletes.
turns.zh: 嗯，肯定不会是那种。奥运会以场馆干净著称。如果你去过奥运会、看过比赛场地，你会注意到场地里没有任何企业广告。任何你能看到运动员比赛的地方，都完全没有企业广告。这算是奥运的一条规则，人人都遵守。如果非要有什么广告，那也是品牌，而品牌是在场外的。可能是在运动员戴头盔的地方之类的。是的。但它非常非常独特，就是彻底干净。你会觉得，哇，这一切都是围绕体育、围绕运动员的。

turns.en: Let's talk about the media landscape, because you've been a dealmaker in that space for a long time. And I got first got my interest in markets during the dotcom bubble. And the weird thing now, and we were talking about this a little bit backstage. is this dynamic where the public companies don't feel like the incumbents in some way. And the incumbents, and I'm talking about AI specifically, feel like the private companies. And I'm curious how much that changes the business of dealmaking. This very strange condition where it's not going to be the public companies making the big acquisitions, etc.
turns.zh: 我们来聊聊媒体版图吧，因为你在这个领域做交易人已经很久了。我最开始对市场的兴趣，是在互联网泡沫（dotcom bubble）那阵子产生的。而现在有个很微妙的现象——我们刚才在后台也聊到了一点——就是这种：上市公司在某种意义上反倒不像那些在位的巨头（incumbents），而在位的巨头——我说的尤其是 AI——反倒像是私募公司。我很好奇，这在多大程度上改变了做交易这门生意。这是一种很奇怪的状况：将来做大型收购的不会是那些上市公司，等等。

turns.en: It's like something is completely flipped.
turns.zh: 就好像有什么东西被彻底颠倒过来了。

turns.en: Well, on the one hand, this is the biggest M & A year in the history of the world.
turns.zh: 嗯，一方面，这是世界历史上最大的一年并购（M&A）。

turns.en: Really?
turns.zh: 真的吗？

turns.en: Biggest year by far. We expect the M & A market to be much bigger than it was at the peak. The last peak was 2021, inflated by COVID.
turns.zh: 而且是遥遥领先的最大年份。我们预计今年的并购市场会远远大于上一个峰值。上一个峰值是 2021 年，被 COVID 给抬高了。

turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: So just keep that in mind. And it's deep. And for the past several years, 40% of the M & A market has been selling companies that were owned by private equity sponsors.
turns.zh: 所以你得把这点记在心里。而且它很有深度。过去这几年里，并购市场的 40% 都是在出售由私募基金（private equity sponsors）持有的公司。

turns.en: This year, that's 30%. And the reason is there's so much more substantive demand with things that are happening around the technology impact of the economy in every possible way. And you think about it, every industry, natural resources or power generation, they're experiencing the same thing, again, because they're building the infrastructure for AI. We've seen an enormous boom in semiconductor technology, semiconductor equities and semiconductor M & A when everybody wants to have proprietary semiconductor technology. So what's what's driving the M & A market is the same phenomenon that we see driving interest in almost everything. And it's actually incredibly strong.
turns.zh: 今年这个比例是 30%。原因在于，围绕着科技对经济方方面面的影响，正在发生的事带来了多得多的、更实质的需求。你想想看，每个行业——自然资源、发电——都在经历同样的事情，还是因为他们在为 AI 建基础设施。我们看到了半导体技术、半导体股票和半导体并购的巨大繁荣，因为人人都想拥有自研的半导体技术。所以真正驱动并购市场的，正是我们看到的那个几乎在驱动一切兴趣的同一个现象。而且它实际上极其强劲。

turns.en: Can companies buy their way into, I guess, like AI fluency or nativity? Because you see, I was reading the Goldman Sachs M & A Outlook on the beach, which is the best place to read it. And you were talking about DNA deals and this idea.
turns.zh: 公司能不能靠收购买到——我猜是——AI 的流利度或者'原生能力'？因为你知道，我当时在海滩上读 Goldman Sachs 的并购展望报告，那可是读它的最佳地点。你们在里面讲到了 DNA 交易（DNA deals）和这个理念。

turns.en: Don't get sand on our stuff. Sorry.
turns.zh: 别把沙子弄到我们的东西上。抱歉。

turns.en: And you were talking about this idea that like a lot of the M & A activity is being driven by companies that want more of a foothold in AI. But then when I look at larger companies, it really does feel like it's a challenge for big incumbent companies to integrate AI into their existing organization. And sometimes it feels a lot easier for the startups to just start from scratch and say, we're an AI company. We're building this from the ground up.
turns.zh: 你们讲到的这个理念是说，很多并购活动是那些想在 AI 里占更多立足点的公司在推动的。但当我看那些大公司时，感觉把 AI 整合进现有的组织，对大型在位巨头来说真的是个难题。有时候感觉对初创公司来说要容易得多，它们干脆从零开始，说'我们是一家 AI 公司，我们从底层就把这个建起来。'

turns.en: Well, every startup, even in AI, has to think to themselves, what's the end game? And for 80% of the startups, the end game is selling themselves to somebody else. So I think that's in the mind of the entrepreneur who is the founder. and the venture capitalists who are financing the entrepreneur, that's sort of the economic payoff of actually building something innovative. You have to think, how does what I'm building help somebody else who has some other part of the puzzle? And so I think that's actually present in every kind of entrepreneurial investment, every entrepreneurial venture. that the 20% that actually become sustained companies, they have something totally differentiated, or frankly, they would never be able to find somebody who could buy them. And you think about SpaceX. SpaceX did something different And they did something different in a market where there were lots of incumbents, but the incumbents played in a regulatory environment that SpaceX decided to defy. And it's that kind of differentiation that leads to a company that becomes an independent company. I think we'll see, obviously, Anthropic and OpenAI be independent companies. They're almost too big for anybody to buy. And so that's the other part of this. If the companies do become too big, they've succeeded very, very well. But you just have to have a lot of confidence that they're going to have a durable platform.
turns.zh: 嗯，每一家初创公司，哪怕是在 AI 领域，都得自己想清楚：终局（end game）是什么？而对 80% 的初创公司来说，终局就是把自己卖给别的公司。所以我觉得，这正是那位作为创始人的创业者脑子里想的，也是那些给创业者出资的风险投资人想的——这才是真正做出创新东西之后的经济回报。你得想，我正在建的这个东西，怎么帮到某个手里握着拼图另一块的人？所以我觉得这实际上存在于每一种创业型投资、每一桩创业冒险里。而那 20% 真正成长为可持续公司的，它们都有某种彻底差异化的东西，或者说白了，要不然它们根本找不到能买下自己的人。你想想 SpaceX。SpaceX 做了不一样的事，而且是在一个有很多在位巨头的市场里做了不一样的事——但那些在位者是在一个 SpaceX 决定不去服从的监管环境里玩的。正是这种差异化，造就了一家最终独立出来的公司。我觉得我们显然会看到 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 成为独立公司。它们几乎大到没人买得起了。所以这也是另一面：如果这些公司真的变得太大，那它们就是非常非常成功了。但你得很有信心，相信它们会有一个能持久的平台。

turns.en: Am I going to read an S-1 one day and when you list through the risk factors that one of the risks is we believe there is a non-trivial chance that our technology wipes out the entirety of humanity? Is that the type of thing the lawyers are going to make them put in?
turns.zh: 将来有一天我会不会读到一份 S-1，然后在你列的风险因素里，其中一条风险是'我们相信，我们的技术有相当大的可能会把全人类消灭殆尽'？律师会不会逼着他们把这种东西写进去？

turns.en: I think the lawyers will probably say you better protect yourself and make sure that the disclosure is complete. So imagine... Big, crazy, scary things like that will be present in S1 language for sure.
turns.zh: 我觉得律师大概会说，你最好保护好自己，确保披露是完整的。所以想象一下……像那种又大、又疯狂、又吓人的东西，肯定会出现在 S-1 的措辞里。

turns.en: I've always thought if people only read the S1s, they would never invest in another company because they're always so frightening.
turns.zh: 我一直觉得，如果人们只读 S-1 的话，他们再也不会投资任何一家公司了，因为它们总是那么吓人。

turns.en: Maybe that's a sad comment about what people read.
turns.zh: 也许这是对人们都读些什么的一句悲哀的评语吧。

turns.en: That's probably the case.
turns.zh: 很可能就是这样。

turns.en: Wait, when I read an S1, I always flip straight to the risk factors. Is that bad?
turns.zh: 等等，我读 S-1 的时候，总是直接翻到风险因素那部分。这样不好吗？

turns.en: We always do that. That's what we always do.
turns.zh: 我们从来都这么干。这就是我们一贯的做法。

turns.en: We always want to see that. It's our natural draw. It's a risk. No, no, that's the journalist prerogative. That's the journalist prerogative. Fair enough.
turns.zh: 我们一直就想看那个。那是我们的天然吸引。这是风险嘛。不不，那是记者的特权。那是记者的特权。也说得过去。

turns.en: Given your TMT experience, you know, a lot of people have been drawing parallels between what's going on in AI right now with the TMT build out and everyone was excited about the web. And so we laid loads and loads of cable and directionally we were kind of right. The Internet did in fact become a thing.
turns.zh: 以你在 TMT（科技、媒体、电信）领域的经验，你知道，很多人一直在把眼下 AI 里发生的事跟当年的 TMT 大建设做类比，那时候人人都为互联网兴奋。于是我们铺了海量的光缆，而大方向上我们其实是对的。互联网确实成了气候。

turns.en: It all got used eventually.
turns.zh: 最后全都被用上了。

turns.en: It all got used eventually. But in the meantime, there was a big bubble. Do you see parallels between what's happening now?
turns.zh: 最后全都被用上了。但在那中间，出现了一个大泡沫。你会不会看到眼下正在发生的事跟当年有相似之处？

turns.en: Well, certainly there's no way to know for sure how big is this market going to be? And are we committing to build too much infrastructure relative to the real demand that we're going to see five or six years from now? I think the answer is we just don't know. I will say the people financing the investments are not just venture capitalists who are the principal investors. in the first build out of the TMT internet phase in sort of 2000, 2001. Now the investors in this build out are the most successful big technology platforms anywhere in the world who had hundreds of billions of dollars of free cash flow until this year. So it's an incredible turnabout.
turns.zh: 嗯，当然，没法百分百确定这个市场到底会有多大，也没法确定相对于五六年后我们会真正看到的需求，我们是不是承诺建了太多基础设施。我觉得答案就是我们根本不知道。我要说的是，为这些投资出钱的人，已经不只是风险投资人了——在大约 2000、2001 年 TMT 互联网那一轮首次大建设里，风险投资人才是主要的投资者。而现在这一轮建设里的投资者，是全世界最成功的那些大型科技平台，它们在今年之前手里有几千亿美元的自由现金流。所以这是一次令人难以置信的反转。

turns.en: I have this theory and tell me if I'm wrong, that actually enterprise AI adoption is literally zero.
turns.zh: 我有一个理论，说错了你别笑话我：其实企业级 AI 的采用率基本是零。

turns.en: And what I mean by that 2%, not 2%.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，2%，连 2% 都不到。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: Well, no, we just did an analysis and we said it's 2% today.
turns.zh: 呃，不，我们刚做了一项分析，得出的结论是眼下有 2%。

turns.en: And what I mean, at least.
turns.zh: 我是说，至少吧。

turns.en: In my mind is like, sure.
turns.zh: 在我脑子里就是这种，行吧。

turns.en: Has every company gotten their employees like a chat GPT or Claude subscription?
turns.zh: 有没有哪家公司给员工都配了个 ChatGPT 或者 Claude 的订阅？

turns.en: Yeah, sure. Probably.
turns.zh: 有，当然。大概有。

turns.en: But like, you know, if it's the if it's the usage of like, oh, I'm going on the Oddlots podcast, who are these Joe and Tracy fellows? What do they ask questions like? I don't really consider that AI adoption in a meaningful sense. That's a glorified search.
turns.zh: 但你知道，如果所谓的用法就是，'哦，我要上 OddLots 播客了，Joe 和 Tracy 这俩是谁啊？他们都问些什么问题？'这种我不认为是有意义的 AI 采用。那是个华丽版的搜索而已。

turns.en: When you look at companies. in the range. Have you seen any sense in which incumbent.
turns.zh: 当你看那些在这个区间里的公司。你有没有看到在位巨头在某种意义上——

turns.en: Companies are deeply building AI into the workflow such that it's not just a window on a computer screen that they can ask questions?
turns.zh: 有没有在位公司在深度地把 AI 建进工作流程里，而不只是在电脑屏幕上开个能问问题的窗口？

turns.en: So 2% are the companies who in their earnings reports have said, we see an impact on EPS, a positive impact of our use of AI, 2% so far. There are probably 20 or 30% of the companies that have actually implemented strategies to use AI in everything they do. I mean, I think about Goldman Sachs. We are. You know, we have enormous numbers of prompts about things that we use AI to do. And all of the people who are the youngest people at Goldman Sachs are sort of native AI people working to implement things that we didn't think about a year ago. And now we've found that we can give people more capacity more quickly and get them to think about different types of problems than we did, as I say, even a year ago. So we're beginning to see how it changes the way people work with each other and what they imagine they can achieve.
turns.zh: 所以那 2%，是那些在财报里说过'我们看到 AI 的使用对每股收益（EPS）有影响、有正面影响'的公司，到目前为止是 2%。真正已经落地战略、把 AI 用到自己做的每一件事里的公司，大概有 20% 到 30%。我是说，你想想 Goldman Sachs。我们就是。你知道，我们有海量的提示词（prompts），涉及我们用 AI 去做的各种事。而在 Goldman Sachs 最年轻的那批人，都算是 AI 原生的人，他们在落地一些我们一年前根本想不到的东西。现在我们发现，我们能更快地给人腾出更多精力，让他们去思考跟以往不同类型的问题——就像我说的，哪怕跟一年前比也一样。所以我们开始看到，它是怎么改变人与人之间协作的方式、以及他们觉得自己能达成什么的。

turns.en: Wait, say more about AI in the deal making business specifically, because I imagine, yes, there are a bunch of junior analysts who are using it to make PowerPoints look even more beautiful than they already do and Excel spreadsheets. And maybe you're even searching for like potential targets with an AI prompt or something like that. But the other thing you always hear about M & A is ultimately it's a relationship business. What would you expect actual integrated AI use to look like in the M & A space?
turns.zh: 等等，多讲讲 AI 具体在做交易这门生意里的应用，因为我想，是有一堆初级分析师在用它把 PowerPoint 做得比原本还要漂亮，还有 Excel 表格。也许你们甚至还会用一个 AI 提示词去搜潜在的收购标的之类的。但关于并购，你还总会听到一点：它归根结底是一门关系的生意。你会预期在并购领域，真正把 AI 整合进去的用法长什么样？

turns.en: I think M & A is a business of using trusted relationships and good advice. People are looking for someone who understands the world and is able to synthesize a lot of independent variables. synthesizing independent variables, it's a gift that many people have. If they're good at this, they will be better at it if they use AI. They'll be faster at getting to conclusions. They'll be more imaginative at saying, well, this is the first data point that I was able to get when I asked this question, but I don't exactly feel confident that's the right answer. Let me go ask the counter question. And so I think people become, it's not that they're becoming smarter, it's if they have access to more information, better information, and that allows them to have more confidence and better judgment. And I actually think it will shape the way everybody in this field provides advice and thinks about what the expectations of the clients are going to be.
turns.zh: 我觉得并购是一门靠可信的关系和好的建议来做的生意。人们在找的是那种既懂这个世界、又能把大量相互独立的变量综合起来的人。综合这些独立的变量，这是一种很多人具备的天赋。如果他们本来就擅长这个，那么用了 AI 之后他们会更擅长。他们下结论会更快。他们会更有想象力，会说，'嗯，这是我问这个问题时能拿到的第一个数据点，但我不太确定这就是正确答案，让我再去问那个反面的问题。'所以我觉得，人们并不是在变得更聪明，而是——如果他们能拿到更多信息、更好的信息，这就让他们更有底气、判断力更好。而且我真的觉得，它会塑造这个领域里每一个人提供建议的方式，以及他们对客户会有什么样的预期。

turns.en: You know, on media specifically, setting aside the deal-making question, I could see two totally– there's probably ten, but two totally different visions of what AI could mean for media. So there is the one view. It's like anyone could be a media maker right now. Anyone could make video right now from their home office, and therefore the value of media becomes less valuable.
turns.zh: 你知道，就媒体这块而言，先把做交易的问题放一边，我能看到两种——可能有十种，但两种——关于 AI 对媒体意味着什么的截然不同的设想。有一种设想是这样的：现在任何人都能成为媒体创作者。任何人都能在自己家里的书房做视频，因此媒体的价值就变得更不值钱了。

turns.en: It's commoditized.
turns.zh: 它被商品化了（commoditized）。

turns.en: The other version I could see is if you have IP, if you have a name, if you have et cetera, AI could be this force multiplier. Maybe Tom Cruise will license nine versions of Tom Cruise and Tom Cruise could be in 10 movies.
turns.zh: 我能看到的另一个版本是：如果你手里有 IP、有名号等等，AI 可能是这种力量放大器。也许 Tom Cruise 会授权九个版本的 Tom Cruise，然后 Tom Cruise 就能同时出现在 10 部电影里。

turns.en: Are we sure that's not already happening, Jim?
turns.zh: 我们确定这不是已经在发生了吗，Jim？

turns.en: It may already be happening.
turns.zh: 它可能已经在发生了。

turns.en: I'm curious whether the clients that you talk to are more of like, I'm very anxious. This is like anyone could do what before I took years to build a giant lot in Hollywood and now it could be done on some computer versus I own this thing and I have so many more ways to make it extensible.
turns.zh: 我很好奇，你接触的那些客户，更多是那种'我很焦虑'——就像，以前我要在 Hollywood 建一个巨大的片场得花好几年，现在任何人都能在某台电脑上做到——还是那种'我拥有这个东西，而且我多了好多办法把它延展出去'？

turns.en: Depends on how self-confident the client is. Okay. I would say if you look at incumbents in the music industry, they're very anxious about bandit AI upending something that's been seasoned and built over a long period of time. So they look at how do I protect myself against somebody misusing content that was created by me or one of my clients or one of the people that I represent or I have a license with. So I think that's got to get sorted out. At the same time, if you are the creator and you think, well, I just have a tool that makes my creativity that much more potent. And I'm going to do something I only imagined about doing, but I could never figure out how to do it myself. Suddenly, I can create music with themes and experiences that I don't have the competence to do on my own, but I can figure out how to get it. And that's incredibly powerful. And I believe that will be a phenomenon that impacts how media is both created and what becomes popular and people's expectations for how do they get entertained? What's going to be vivid enough that they want to buy it or download it?
turns.zh: 这要看客户有多自信。好。我会这么说，如果你看音乐行业的在位巨头，他们非常焦虑，怕那种'强盗式 AI'（bandit AI）颠覆某个经过长期打磨、长期积累起来的东西。所以他们在琢磨，我怎么保护自己，防止有人滥用由我、或我的某个客户、或我代理的某个人、或跟我签了授权的人所创作的内容。所以我觉得这一点得先理清楚。与此同时，如果你就是那个创作者，你会想，'嗯，我只是多了一件工具，让我的创造力变得更强大了。我要去做一件我原本只是想象过、却从来没能自己搞明白怎么做的事。'突然间，我就能创作出带有某些主题和体验的音乐，那些是我自己没本事做出来的，但我能想办法把它弄出来。这是极其强大的。而且我相信，这会成为一个现象，影响到媒体是怎么被创作出来的、什么会变得流行，以及人们对'怎么被娱乐'的预期——什么东西得足够生动，他们才愿意去买、去下载？

turns.en: Do you have a sense of whether back catalogs or libraries of content are getting more valuable or less valuable right now?
turns.zh: 你有没有感觉到，眼下那些老作品库（back catalogs）或者内容库是变得更值钱了，还是更不值钱了？

turns.en: Well, they have been getting more valuable over the past, let's say, 10 years. In part, you've had people who want to securitize the cash flows coming from them, right? I actually think that there is a lot to be said for familiarity and things that have already been seasoned and they're widely appreciated. So I actually think it will get more valuable. And I think AI is likely to make existing contents in catalogs more valuable because it will find more uses for existing content. We're going to be, maybe AI will create an environment in which we're going to find it will be pulsed by different types of media content in ways we never imagined before. And rather than be barraged by it and resent it, AI is going to be smart enough to theoretically How do I do this so it's actually appealing to people? You think about maybe a progenitor of AI. It is actually created with all the same tools. What makes TikTok so attractive to people? Why are people drawn to TikToks? It's because the algorithms designed by Yiping Zhang a decade ago and the teams that he built in China to develop the way that the system worked was incredibly positive. He is, by the way, the one person who would say he is the only Chinese person or only Chinese company to have created something that the rest of the world really wants to buy because it's totally unique and it was developed there.
turns.zh: 嗯，在过去——就说 10 年吧——它们一直在变得更值钱。部分原因是，有人想把这些内容带来的现金流证券化（securitize），对吧？我其实觉得，对于那种耳熟能详、已经被时间检验过、又被广泛喜爱的东西，是很有话可说的。所以我认为它会变得更值钱。而且我觉得 AI 很可能会让曲库里现有的内容更值钱，因为它会为现有内容找到更多用途。我们将来会——也许 AI 会创造出一种环境，让我们发现，它会以我们前所未想的方式，被不同类型的媒体内容所驱动、所激发。而与其被它轰炸、对它反感，AI 理论上会聪明到——我怎么做才能让这东西真正吸引到人？你想想，也许 AI 的一个前身，其实是用一整套同样的工具创造出来的。是什么让 TikTok 对人们如此有吸引力？为什么人们会被 TikTok 吸引？那是因为十年前由 Yiping Zhang 设计的算法、以及他在中国组建的那些团队所开发的系统运作方式，极其正面。顺便说一句，他就是那种唯一会说'自己是唯一创造出一样全世界都真心想买的东西的中国人或中国公司'的人，因为那东西完全独一无二，而且是在那里开发出来的。

turns.en: Yeah, it's really extraordinary and it's really a breakthrough. If Tracy and I went to L.A., could we find a startup agent or et cetera pitching us on the idea that like, let me clone your voice and have you could produce 10x the content?
turns.zh: 是啊，这真的很非凡，也真的是一个突破。如果 Tracy 和我去了 L.A.，我们会不会碰到某个创业公司经纪人之类的，来向我们推销一个点子，比如'让我克隆你的声音，你就能产出 10 倍的内容'？

turns.en: Is that a thing that's happening right now?
turns.zh: 这是眼下正在发生的事吗？

turns.en: I believe it is. I believe you'll find lots of people encouraging you to try things that are out of your comfort zone, but have great upside potential.
turns.zh: 我相信是的。我相信你会发现一大堆人在鼓励你去尝试那些超出你舒适区、但有着巨大上行空间的东西。

turns.en: So one of the reasons we wanted to talk to you is you've been in finance for, there are a number of reasons, but you've been in finance for many decades now, I think since the 1980s. So you've lived through multiple cycles of, you know, top of the market and then the inevitable bust. From your vantage point as an M & A guy, you see a lot of deals that come to fruition. I imagine you see a lot of deals that just remain in the sort of talked about stage. Are there certain ideas that you start to see when markets are beginning to get a little bit crazy, a little bit irrational that you think to yourself, well, wait a second, maybe we're getting ahead of our skis a little bit?
turns.zh: 我们想跟你聊的原因之一，是你在金融界已经干了很多个十年了，我想是从 1980 年代开始的。所以你亲历过好几轮周期，你知道，市场见顶、然后是不可避免的崩盘。以一个并购人的视角，你会看到很多交易最终落地。我想你也会看到很多交易就停留在'被谈论'的阶段。当市场开始变得有点疯狂、有点失去理智时，有没有某些念头是你一看到就会心想'等等，也许我们有点超前、有点冲昏头了'的？

turns.en: It's interesting. I think there's not a frenzy, but an appetite for deals right now on the part of people who think about changing what they have or making it better by doing a deal that they didn't imagine they would be able to get done five years ago. There's a sense that now the world is open to this kind of transaction. And if you don't do it, you're probably going to lose the opportunity. This is not something that we found is a persistent condition. There will be other things that get in the way. The financial markets won't be as open. You'll have a regulatory environment that would be more resistant. So I actually think the bias on the part of corporate boards and decision makers is to be pro-deal in a way that we see from time to time. But I don't think we see it as something that lasts forever. You have to take advantage of it when it's there.
turns.zh: 这很有意思。我觉得眼下并不是有一股狂热，而是一种对交易的胃口——来自那些琢磨着通过做一笔交易来改变或改善自己现有资产的人，而这种交易五年前他们还想象不到自己能做成。有一种感觉是，现在整个世界对这类交易是敞开的，而如果你不做，你很可能就会错失这个机会。这并不是一件我们发现的、会长期持续存在的状态。会有别的东西冒出来挡路。金融市场不会那么敞开。你会碰到一个更具抵触性的监管环境。所以我其实觉得，公司董事会和决策者身上那种偏向，是倾向于支持交易的——这种偏向我们时不时会看到。但我不认为它是那种能永远持续下去的东西。当它出现的时候，你得抓住。

turns.en: I have one last question. A friend of mine said something to me very interesting. We use this term M & A.
turns.zh: 我还有最后一个问题。我一个朋友跟我说过一件很有意思的事。我们用'并购（M&A）'这个词。

turns.en: It's come up.
turns.zh: 它冒出来了。

turns.en: And he does M & A professionally. He's like, you know, Joe, it's just A. There's no mergers anymore.
turns.zh: 而他就是专业做并购的。他说，'你知道吗，Joe，那其实只是 A（收购）。已经没有 M（合并）了。'

turns.en: And I started thinking, I was like, yeah, it's a Citigroup Travelers.
turns.zh: 然后我就开始琢磨，我想，是啊，是那种 Citigroup 和 Travelers 的合并。

turns.en: That's old.
turns.zh: 那太老古董了。

turns.en: Wait, but this was always true.
turns.zh: 等等，但这一直以来都是这样啊。

turns.en: Whenever there was a merger, someone would always be acquiring someone else.
turns.zh: 每当有一桩合并，总有一方是在收购另一方。

turns.en: But almost it all seems acquisitions. Are there still the M's?
turns.zh: 但几乎全都是收购。那些 M 还在吗？

turns.en: Look, M is just a way of describing you're putting two companies together that generally are in the same size category.
turns.zh: 听着，M 只是一种描述方式，说的是你把两家公司合到一起，它们通常属于同一档规模。

turns.en: Roughly the same size, yeah.
turns.zh: 大致相同的规模，对。

turns.en: And then sometimes you'll end up with board members coming from both sides and you split the management teams. That part of M never lasts. There are things that are done to make the deal happen. You're giving people the space to say, I think this is a smart thing to do. I was able to sell at a premium or I was able to merge at a premium. So my shareholders will be comfortable. But a year after the deal is done, you have to get used to the world that you have and leadership and the influence to make decisions for the company. tends to consolidate into a set of hands that may not be exactly where you started.
turns.zh: 然后有时候你会以双方都派人进董事会告终，你会把管理团队拆分。M 的那一部分从来长久不了。那些做法是为了让交易达成而做的。你是在给人们空间去说，'我觉得这是件明智的事。我要么能以溢价卖掉，要么能以溢价合并，所以我的股东会安心。'但交易做成一年之后，你就得习惯你手里拥有的这个世界了，而领导权、以及为公司做决策的影响力，往往会集中到某一拨人手里，而这拨人可能跟你最初设想的不完全一样。

turns.en: All right, Gene Sykes, thank you so much for coming on Odd Lots. Thank you, Future Proof, for having us once again. And thank you to our lovely audience. Really appreciate you being here today.
turns.zh: 好的，Gene Sykes，非常感谢你上 Odd Lots。也谢谢 Future Proof 再次邀请我们。还有谢谢我们可爱的观众。真的很感激你们今天到场。

turns.en: Thank you so much.
turns.zh: 非常感谢。

turns.en: Thank you. That was our conversation with Gene Sykes, recorded live at the Future Proof Conference.
turns.zh: 谢谢。这就是我们与 Gene Sykes 的那段对话，是在 Future Proof 大会现场录制的。

turns.en: Really enjoyed it. Learned a lot. I am more inclined to maybe come.
turns.zh: 我真的很享受，学到很多。我更倾向于也许可以去一趟。

turns.en: I was going to say, this is the question. Are you going to come in 2028?
turns.zh: 我正要说呢，问题就在这儿。你 2028 年要去吗？

turns.en: I still think it sounds like a mess, but he made a pretty compelling sales... I mean, he's a banker at Goldman Sachs. If there's someone who I would expect to be able to make a pretty compelling sales pitch, it would be him. But maybe it won't be the total mess that I have in my head of what it'd be.
turns.zh: 我还是觉得它听起来会是一团糟，但他做了一番挺有说服力的推销……我是说，他是 Goldman Sachs 的银行家。如果说有什么人我会指望他能做出一番挺有说服力的推销，那就是他了。但也许它不会是我脑子里设想的那种一团糟的样子。

turns.en: So.
turns.zh: 所以嘛。

turns.en: I'm open to it.
turns.zh: 我是持开放态度的。

turns.en: I'm going to watch it on TV and contribute to the air rights financing.
turns.zh: 我打算在电视上看，顺便为转播权的融资贡献一份力。

turns.en: You know what I might do? I might get some really cheap tickets, like the kayaking event or something like that. Or ping pong would be really fun and probably not too expensive compared to, say, track and field.
turns.zh: 你知道我可能会怎么干吗？我可能会去买些特别便宜的票，比如皮划艇项目之类的。或者乒乓球会很有意思，而且跟田径比，大概也不会太贵。

turns.en: So.
turns.zh: 所以嘛。

turns.en: I'm open to it.
turns.zh: 我是持开放态度的。

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: Shall we leave it there for now?
turns.zh: 我们先聊到这儿好吗？

turns.en: Let's leave it there.
turns.zh: 那就聊到这儿。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: This has been another episode of the All Thoughts Podcast. I'm Tracy Allaway. You can follow me at Tracy Allaway.
turns.zh: 这里是又一期的 All Thoughts 播客。我是 Tracy Allaway。你可以在 Tracy Allaway 上关注我。

turns.en: And I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.zh: 你可以在 The Stalwart 上关注我。

turns.zh: 关注我们的制作人：Carmen Rodriguez，账号 Carmen Arman；Dashiell Bennett，账号 Dashbot；Kale Brooks，账号 Kale Brooks；还有 Kevin Lozano，账号 Kevin Lloyd Lozano。

turns.zh: 想看更多 OddLots 的内容，你应该去看看我们的每日通讯（daily newsletter）。你可以在 Bloomberg.com/OddLots 找到它。

turns.en: And you can chat about all of these topics 24-7 in our Discord, Discord.gg slash OddLots.
turns.zh: 你还可以在我们的 Discord 里全天候畅聊所有这些话题，Discord.gg/OddLots。

turns.en: And if you enjoyed this conversation, then please like the video or leave a comment or better yet, subscribe.
turns.zh: 如果你喜欢这段对话，请给视频点个赞、留个言，或者更好——订阅。

turns.en: Thanks for watching and listening.
turns.zh: 感谢你的收看和收听。

turns.en: So so
turns.zh: 就这样，就这样。
